candidate: Noise for the keep rule pooled over all seed panels (kit-native)
what: The loop's margin uses a noise estimate pooled over every full seed panel the campaign has trained, the change's own included, with a multiplier from Student's t at the pooled degrees of freedom.
problem_here: nnloop takes the standard deviation of the baseline panel alone (three runs in the benchmark), so the margin moves with luck: 0.0089 and 0.0052 in two campaigns of the same task and code on 2026-11-11.
mechanism: Pool the within-panel variance over the panels already trained (degrees of freedom add up); take the multiplier from the t distribution at those degrees of freedom; keep the margin formula.
evidence: Measured here on 2026-11-11 from the pilot's two loop campaigns: baseline-panel sd 0.0055 and 0.0032, pooled within-commit sd 0.0048 (6 degrees of freedom) and 0.0029 (4). Monte Carlo (normal noise, independent runs, 40,000 trials per cell, three seeds): the rule as it was coded keeps a change with no effect in 7.9 % of cases, the pooled rule as built in 2.4 %. The price is power early in a campaign: a gain of two deviations is kept in 44 % of cases at the first change and in 58 % after eight earlier panels, against 68 % for the old rule, whose figure includes its false keeps. Details: docs/upgrade/scout/draft/second-look.md and references/loop.md, 'The keep rule'
maturity: Standard statistics; the measurements are from one task on one machine.
cost: No extra runs; some tens of lines in nnloop.py and its tests.
simpler_alternative: Train the baseline on twice as many seeds, which costs runs at every start and after every keep.
reason: Validity: under these assumptions the rule keeps a change with no effect about four times as often as its margin suggests, and the fix needs no extra compute.

candidate: Keep rule that compares a change with the best commit seed by seed (kit-native)
what: The keep rule tests the per-seed differences between a change and the best commit instead of the difference of the two means.
problem_here: nnloop trains a change on the same seeds as the best commit but ignores which run had which seed, so noise that a seed causes in both runs alike is not removed.
mechanism: A paired t-test over the seeds of the panel: the noise is the deviation of the per-seed differences.
evidence: Round 2 (2026-11-12): two commits of the benchmark, 8 seeds, 2 repeats, 30 s budget: correlation of the seed means +0.295 (eight seeds need 0.62 to tell it from chance); sd of the per-seed differences 0.0115, against 0.0136 if seeds shared nothing; sd between seeds 0.0106 and 0.0085, between repeats of one seed 0.00013 and 0.0049. uncertainty.md says how to check this before a paired comparison by hand. Before round 2: Measured here on 2026-11-11 on the pilot's test split, three seeds: the two scripts that differ from the shipped one only by a weight average score 0.0078 and 0.0050 better with a paired sd of 0.0039 and 0.0033, while the unpaired sd over seeds is 0.012 to 0.015. For scripts that change the training trajectory the pairing did not help in the same data. Details: docs/upgrade/scout/draft/second-look.md
maturity: Standard statistics; the measurements are from two campaigns of one task on one machine.
cost: No extra runs. The deviation of the differences depends on the change (how much of a seed's effect it shares with the best commit), so it cannot be pooled over a campaign as the within-panel variance is: with three seeds a paired test has two degrees of freedom (multiplier 4.53 at the rule's error rate, against 2.87 for the pooled test at the first change).
simpler_alternative: The pooled test on the means, which is built.
reason: Measured on the benchmark on 12 Nov 2026: the per-seed scores of two commits do not move together (r = +0.30 over eight seeds, each run twice), so a paired test only loses degrees of freedom. The third report (A1) called the unpaired margin a defect; the measurement does not support that.
cheap_local_trial: Test it still needs: for every change that ran on all seeds, in the ledgers of several campaigns on at least two tasks, compare the deviation of the per-seed differences with the pooled deviation, and simulate both rules on those figures. Not run: only the pilot's campaigns on one task exist, and further campaigns cost agent usage, which is limited.

candidate: Confirmation run by the harness at the end of a campaign: start and kept commit on fresh seeds, with the count of ideas tried (kit-native)
what: When a campaign ends, the harness trains the start commit and the kept commit on seeds outside the panel and reports the gain with an interval and the number of hypotheses the campaign tried.
problem_here: references/loop.md tells the user to do this by hand after a campaign; nothing runs it, so the figure a campaign reports is the selected one, which is biased upward.
mechanism: A confirm step of nnloop, counted against the run limit, with seeds the harness draws; the result goes into the ledger and the journal entry.
evidence: arXiv 2507.02554 (AIRA-dojo, revised 2025-11-04): choosing the final candidate on test instead of validation scores was worth 9 to 13 points of medal rate, nearly all of it at the final choice, and submitting about three top candidates by validation recovered about 10 %. arXiv 2605.17373 (FML-bench, 2026-05-29): mean validation-to-test gap 0.025 to 0.045 across six agents. Both opened by a research subagent on 2026-11-11, not cross-checked. Here: the loop's validation gains of 0.013 and 0.009 on 2026-11-11 were about 0.009 on the test split.
maturity: Standard practice; the same idea is in the rows on a confirmation rule with fresh seeds (sweep-llm-training) and a confirmation holdout (sweep-search-tracking).
cost: Twice the number of fresh seeds in training runs, inside the campaign's run limit.
reason: A campaign's report should carry a gain that selection has not inflated; the published losses at the final choice are larger than those from the search policy.

candidate: Seed escalation for near-misses: a sequential keep rule, up to six seeds, keep at z above 2.4, drop when behind (kit-native)
what: A candidate that is ahead but inside the margin gets further seeds instead of being reverted, until it clears a threshold set for repeated looks or falls behind.
problem_here: With three seeds a real gain as large as the run-to-run noise is kept about one time in five when the noise is known; the idea and the agent session that produced it are then lost.
mechanism: After each seed: z = mean paired difference / (sd * sqrt(2/k)); keep from the third seed on when z > 2.4; drop when z < -0.5 on the first seed or z < 0 later; stop at six seeds. The baseline needs the same six seeds.
evidence: Round 2 (2026-11-12), simulated campaigns (20,000 per setting; true gain of the final commit in run-to-run sd), one look against second panel: 3.96 and 4.02 when runs are the limit, 2.40 and 2.72 when ideas are; ideas with no effect kept 0.90 % and 0.87 %. Not measured on the benchmark. Two poorer mixes of ideas: 1.08 and 1.19, 0.74 and 0.88 (runs); 0.64 and 0.79, 0.48 and 0.66 (ideas). One comparison taken alone keeps 2.7 % of changes with no effect, against 2.3 %. Records of nine real campaigns: 1 of 4 inconclusive results lay above two thirds of the margin. Before round 2: Monte Carlo on 2026-11-11 (normal noise, independent runs, sd known, 40,000 trials per cell): keeps 1.7 % of changes with no effect and 30 %, 61 % and 86 % of real gains of 1, 1.5 and 2 run-to-run sd, at 3.1 to 4.4 runs per idea. The three-seed rule with the sd known keeps 2.1 % and 21 %, 42 % and 66 %, at 2.0 to 2.9 runs. Per run the two find real gains at about the same rate; per agent session the sequential rule finds more.
maturity: Group-sequential testing is standard; these boundaries are mine and come from simulation only.
cost: About half as many runs again per idea, plus three more baseline runs per kept commit.
simpler_alternative: A fixed panel of five seeds.
reason: Built on 12 Nov 2026 in a simpler form: one further panel of n seeds when the gain is above two thirds of the margin, then one decision on 2n seeds at 1.1 times the multiplier. In simulation a campaign ends 1.5 % (inside the error) to 38 % further ahead, with no more false keeps per idea.
cheap_local_trial: Two campaigns each way on the benchmark at the same token limit, confirmed gain compared; about 40 minutes of GPU and four campaigns of agent usage.

candidate: Numeric settings searched by the harness inside the loop, code changes left to the agent (hybrid; standard-library random search or successive halving, Optuna when installed)
what: An iteration may declare a few numeric settings with ranges instead of one code change; the harness searches them itself, scores every trial with the frozen evaluator, and puts the winner through the normal keep rule.
problem_here: The loop's agent picks numbers by hand: the two kept changes of 2026-11-11 used weight-average decays of 0.995 and 0.998 without any search.
mechanism: PROPOSAL.json gains an optional search space; the training command takes the values as arguments; the search budget counts against the run limit.
evidence: Measured 2026-11-13 with the stand-in agent on both benchmark tasks, three pairs of campaigns per task at 18 runs: fine-tuning task, confirmed gain 0.42 with the search against 0.31 by hand; character model, nothing kept either way. Off by default. Round 3 (2026-11-12): built and tested with the stand-in agent (tests/test_loop.py, campaign h: a search that finds a gain is kept, the trial runs stay out of the noise estimate and off the seed panels, the run limit counts them). Before round 3: arXiv 2603.24647 v3 (opened by a research subagent on 2026-11-11): nine methods, 24 GPU-hours each, three seeds: CMA-ES with a language model proposing 30 % of trials 0.9763, TPE 0.9768, SMAC 0.9778, CMA-ES 0.9785, the code-editing agent 0.9814, from a baseline near 0.991; out-of-memory failures were 16 % or less for the best methods and 48 to 61 % for the worst; one task and open-weight models (authors' caveat). The rows of 10 November cite v5 of the same paper with other figures (0.9739, 0.9768, 0.9770).
maturity: One controlled study on one task; classical optimizers themselves are mature.
cost: A new iteration kind in nnloop.py, a contract for passing values to the training command, tests; the search itself spends runs.
simpler_alternative: Keep references/hpo.md section 8 as advice and run searches outside the loop.
reason: Built on 12 Nov 2026 in a simpler form: opt-in by loop.search_trials; a stratified random search (Latin hypercube) of K versions, each trained once on one seed outside both seed panels, the best one committed by the harness and decided by the unchanged keep rule and confirmation. The values live in the code as lines `NAME = <number>`, not in arguments of the training command, because the confirmation and every later iteration train a commit with the campaign's one command. No successive halving and no Optuna: at a handful of trials the model-based samplers are still in their random start-up phase, and stopping by rank is the riskiest speed-up (references/hpo.md). Why: The only controlled comparison found says a classical optimizer beats a code-editing agent inside a fixed numeric space; the agent's value is in code changes.
cheap_local_trial: On the benchmark at an equal run limit: the loop with the search step against the loop without, two campaigns each, confirmed gain compared; about one hour of GPU.

candidate: Branch on stall: greedy until nothing is kept for k iterations, then restart from an earlier kept commit with a cleared history (adaptive agent of FML-bench, arXiv 2605.17373)
what: The loop stays greedy while it finds gains and branches only when it stalls.
problem_here: Both campaigns of 2026-11-11 kept one change and discarded every other idea from the same starting point.
mechanism: After k iterations without a keep, start the next worktree from the commit before the last keep (or the start), and give the worker a history without the stalled branch.
evidence: Round 3 (2026-11-12): built as loop.restart_after and tested with the stand-in agent of the kit's tests (tests/test_loop.py, campaign r): the restart, the worker's history, the branch, the confirmation and a resume behave as described. Not run: the trial below, which needs campaigns of 40 runs with real agent sessions, two each way. So whether a restart raises what a campaign ends on is not measured. The paper was opened again on 2026-11-12 by a second subagent (v2; the first part read from the page, the method details from a machine summary): its adaptive agent branches from its best few code versions, and no test of the difference between 0.192 and 0.208 was found in what was read. Before round 3: arXiv 2605.17373 (2026-05-29; six agents, 18 tasks, 324 runs, one model for all): mean normalised test improvement 0.192 for the greedy loop, 0.193 for tree search, 0.208 for the agent that starts greedy and branches on a stall. Opened by a research subagent on 2026-11-11, not cross-checked. Related row: Fork-and-Flush (sweep-auto-research).
maturity: Built in round 3; its effect is not measured. One study; small effect.
cost: Small in code, because every iteration already starts in a fresh worktree; needs long campaigns to show anything.
simpler_alternative: Start a second campaign by hand.
reason: Built on 12 Nov 2026 as loop.restart_after in nnloop.py, off unless set: after that many iterations in a row without a keep, the next worktree starts from the commit before the last keep, and the worker reads the history of the code in front of it, with a change that was kept elsewhere marked as not in that code. Added to the mechanism above, because a restart needs them: the commit that is left stays the campaign's result until a keep on the new line beats it on the seed panel, the campaign ends on the best commit it found and confirms that one, and two sessions in a row that decline also start a restart while there is a commit to go back to. It differs from the paper's agent, which branches from its best few code versions: this goes back one keep at a time on a single line. Why: Small measured effect in one study, cheap to build on the existing design.
cheap_local_trial: Campaigns long enough to stall: on the benchmark 40 runs per campaign, two campaigns each way.

candidate: Population search with mutation and crossover over research states (GEAR, arXiv 2605.13874 v1, 2026-05-08)
what: A population of research states replaces the single best commit; new candidates come from mutation and from crossing two members.
problem_here: The loop keeps one line of descent.
evidence: Abstract only, opened by a research subagent on 2026-11-11: claims a gain over the greedy loop at equal compute; the abstract gives no figures.
cost: A population multiplies the runs per idea, which one GPU pays for in wall-clock time.
reason: No figures seen, and the cost falls on the scarce resource of a single-GPU user.
cheap_local_trial: Read the full paper for its figures and compute before any trial.

candidate: Progressive graph search with retrieval memory (MLEvolve, arXiv 2606.06473, 2026-06-04)
what: Monte Carlo graph search over solutions with references across branches and a retrieval memory.
problem_here: Candidate for the loop's search policy.
evidence: arXiv 2606.06473 (opened by a research subagent on 2026-11-11): 65.3 % medals on the 75 tasks of MLE-bench at 12 hours per task; on 22 Lite tasks removing the graph search or the memory each lowered the medal rate from 81.8 % to 68.2 %; the ablations report no seeds, and the paper has no validation-against-test analysis.
reason: Measured on many-task competition work at 12 hours per task. Two controlled studies find a greedy loop level with tree search (arXiv 2605.17373) and the search policy secondary to the set of operations (arXiv 2507.02554). Reopen if the branch-on-stall trial shows a gain.

candidate: Step-counted run budget as a way to lower run-to-run noise on one machine
what: Stop a run after a fixed number of steps instead of a fixed time, so that machine load cannot change how far a run gets.
problem_here: The benchmark trains for a fixed 30 seconds; I suspected that this was a source of the run-to-run noise.
evidence: Measured here on 2026-11-11 in the pilot's two loop campaigns (30-second runs, one otherwise idle GPU): the steps completed vary by 0.1 to 1.4 % within a commit, and their within-commit correlation with the score is +0.31 over nine runs and -0.16 over six.
reason: On one idle machine the time budget is not where the noise comes from. Across machines or under load it still matters: see the row on hardware pinning and step-based budgets (loop-autoresearch).

candidate: Seed panel trained in parallel on one GPU
what: The seeds of one candidate train at the same time when memory allows.
problem_here: The loop trains one run at a time; the benchmark uses a small part of a 32 GB card.
mechanism: Launch the panel together and wait for all of it; needs a budget that does not depend on how many runs share the GPU.
evidence: Vendor blog without repeats (https://skypilot.ai/blog/scaling-autoresearch, 2026-03-18): 16 GPUs reached the same best loss about nine times sooner. Nothing measured for several runs sharing one GPU.
cost: A step-counted budget option and concurrency in nnloop.train.
reason: Could cut the wall-clock time of a decision to about a third for small models, but under a time budget runs that share a GPU complete fewer steps, which changes the result.
cheap_local_trial: On the benchmark: steps completed and score with one, two and three runs at once, under a step-counted budget.

candidate: Language-model fine-tuning track: a runnable LoRA starter script wired to runlog and the frozen evaluator, and a second benchmark task built on it
what: A tested starter for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of a small open model, and a benchmark task that uses it, so that the kit's fine-tuning guidance is exercised and measured.
problem_here: Every live run so far trained the character model from scratch; the fine-tuning references and the pinned fine-tuning packages have not been used for a real run, and the kit's stated focus is language models.
mechanism: An optional module: a script on the pinned Transformers, PEFT and TRL versions with a chat-template check, a frozen evaluator for generated text, and a task for benchmarks/pilot.py.
evidence: Round 3 (2026-11-12): built and run on the kit's test machine (RTX 5090, native Windows, Transformers 5.22.2, PEFT 0.21.2, PyTorch 2.9.1). The baseline scores 0.351 to 0.386 on three seeds run directly, the evaluator gives the same score twice and refuses a folder without an adapter, and one campaign of the loop with the tests' stand-in agent kept a higher learning rate and confirmed it on fresh seeds (0.667 against 0.332, margin 0.029; 12 runs, 13 minutes). Not run: the three-arm comparison of the trial below, which needs real agent sessions, and anything on Linux. So what the kit adds on a fine-tuning task is still not measured. Before round 3: Kit state on 2026-11-11 (ledger, Recommended combination: nothing in the list was used for real training). Related row: pre-launch feasibility gate (sweep-remote-gpu), whose source reports that 63 % of 30,920 fine-tuning experiments gave no valid run.
maturity: Built in round 3; run on one machine.
cost: The fine-tuning packages in a project environment, a model download after a licence check, about an hour of GPU for a first comparison; a day of work.
reason: Built on 12 Nov 2026 as benchmarks/finetune/: a LoRA adapter for SmolLM2-135M-Instruct (Apache-2.0, one pinned revision, fetched once with size and SHA-256, offline afterwards) on Banking77 (CC BY 4.0), 30 seconds a run; a frozen evaluator that loads nothing but a LoRA adapter in safetensors and scores the generated answers by exact match; one chat-template check shared by trainer and evaluator; runlog wired in; a task for new_project.py and pilot.py. Two points differ from the mechanism above: the trainer is a plain PyTorch loop and does not use TRL, because a fixed time budget needs a loop that watches the clock, and the task lives in the kit's checkout beside charlm, so install.py does not copy it into projects. Why: Nothing measured so far says whether the kit helps with fine-tuning a language model, which is its stated purpose.
cheap_local_trial: Build it with a small permissively licensed model and run the three-arm comparison on it.

candidate: SFT on a stronger agent's solved traces as a warm start before RL (TRL examples/sft_agent_traces, commit a76cab3)
what: Run a strong model as the agent on training tasks, keep only the conversations that ended with a correct answer, and fine-tune the small model on them, with the loss on the assistant turns only, before any RL.
problem_here: The LLM reference names distillation trainers but not this cheaper sequence-level route, which is the usual first step when a small model is to act as an agent.
mechanism: Teacher rollouts through the agent itself (same system prompt and tool schemas), a filter on solved tasks, SFTTrainer with assistant_only_loss, evaluation on tasks whose source dataset no training trace used.
evidence: TRL example README (read 2026-11-12, commit a76cab3), the authors' own single runs: Qwen3.5-2B solves 7.6 % of 144 held-out tasks before and 33.3 % after about 500 traces (teacher 71.5 %); on 163 test tasks 5.5 % and 34.4 %. Without the filter on shared source datasets the student scores 17.3 % on clean tasks and 42.4 % on tasks that share a dataset with a trace, so most of the apparent gain was familiarity with the files. Five times the traces add 3 to 4 points, which the README calls within noise.
maturity: Vendor example in the TRL repository; one model pair and one task family; depends on OpenEnv, Harbor tasks and Hugging Face Sandboxes.
cost: As published it runs on paid Hugging Face Jobs and Inference Providers and uploads datasets and models to the Hub. The fine-tuning step alone is about 16 minutes on one H200 for 500 traces.
simpler_alternative: Plain SFT on an existing instruction dataset, which does not teach the agent's own tool schemas.
reason: Large held-out gain with an honest leakage control, but from one vendor example. The kit can run it as an ordinary training run; the lessons to keep are the split by source dataset instead of by task, and the check that the teacher's licence or terms allow training on its outputs (the example picks an Apache-2.0 teacher for that reason).
cheap_local_trial: Fine-tune the example's student on its published traces on the local GPU through expctl, then score held-out tasks. Not run: the scoring step needs Hugging Face Sandboxes on the user's account, and the example uploads to the Hub by default.

candidate: Harness adapters: one LoRA per model and agent harness, trained with RL inside the unmodified harness (harness-hub, Hugging Face blog of 2026-11-06)
what: Small LoRA adapters trained with GRPO on verifiable tasks inside pi, opencode and hermes, so that a small open model makes fewer tool calls in that harness; released for LFM2.5-24B-A2B, LFM3-1.7B and TwIL-8B.
problem_here: Could make a local model a cheaper driver for the kit's loop, or be a training job that a user of the kit wants to run.
mechanism: TRL AsyncGRPOTrainer with tree attention, rank-32 LoRA on all linear layers, 8 rollouts per task; reward is the task's verifier plus a small bonus for fewer tool calls on correct rollouts; rollouts run in sandboxes through OpenEnv and Harbor; a proxy (safeagents) blocks tool calls that look like reward hacking and scores them 0.
evidence: Blog post (read 2026-11-12): held-out sets of 40 and 150 tasks; results described as from smoke training tests, with no figure per model and harness and no interval except +0.0 +/- 4.1 points for the safeagents ablation; final runs still in progress at publication. The authors' later announcement, as quoted by the user and not checked, gives 'up to' 43 % fewer tool calls and 15 % more accuracy for one model on the data-analysis test set. 253 of the 270 new tasks are of one type and 243 come from one source. Training used 2 or 4 H200 GPUs on Hugging Face Jobs. Licences are not stated in the post.
maturity: Open experiment, one week old; adapters for three small models and three harnesses, none of which the kit supports.
cost: Using one: a local model server next to the training on the same GPU. Training one: paid multi-GPU jobs.
simpler_alternative: Keep a hosted model as the loop's agent; for a local agent, the base model without an adapter.
reason: It cannot be applied to the agents the kit drives (Claude Code, Codex and Cursor with hosted models), the kit has no OpenCode or pi port, and the reported gains are the authors' best cases without intervals. Its task checks (the original solution scores full reward twice; doing nothing, a stub and tampered tests score 0) support the kit's rows on evaluator negative controls. Revisit if an OpenCode port is built or the user wants to train such an adapter.

candidate: safeagents and atif-scan (Hugging Face): rule-based checks of an agent's tool calls and trajectories for reward tampering and benchmark leakage
what: safeagents is a proxy between an agent harness and its model that inspects each tool call in 10 to 20 ms and blocks clear reward-hacking attempts; atif-scan screens recorded trajectories for reward tampering and leakage.
problem_here: The loop scans the agent's transcript for tampering with its own short list of patterns; a maintained detector set could find what that list misses.
mechanism: Three stages: the request itself (undeclared tools, hosts not in the conversation), atif-scan detectors plus plugins, and an optional model judge that the authors left off.
evidence: Blog post of 2026-11-06 (read 2026-11-12): in a 50-step ablation the proxy changed held-out pass@1 by +0.0 +/- 4.1 points; one blocked call is shown; the number of blocked attempts is not stated. Neither repository was read.
maturity: New; published with the harness-adapters experiment.
cost: A package, and a conversion of the kit's transcripts to the ATIF format. The proxy needs the agent's model traffic to pass through it, which works for a local model server only.
simpler_alternative: The kit's guard hook, which checks every tool call before it runs, and its transcript scan.
reason: The same idea as the kit's guard and transcript scan, from a vendor that publishes the attempts it blocked; whether its detectors find more than the kit's is untested.
cheap_local_trial: Convert the saved transcripts of the two real loop campaigns to ATIF, run atif-scan on them and on a transcript with a planted evaluator edit, and compare with the kit's scan. Not run: the repositories were not read (usage limit), and a third-party package must be read and pinned first.

what: Hosted service with a plugin for Claude Code, Copilot CLI and Codex that maps an AI agent application as a flow graph, plays scenarios against it with a simulated user, scores them and proposes fixes.
problem_here: None in a training run: it tests an agent application, not a network's weights. It would matter only for judging an agent built on a model the kit trained.
mechanism: Stages: scan the agent, optional production traces, a scenario suite, simulated runs, a fix plan. The plugin signs in through the browser.
evidence: Connect page (read 2026-11-12): the install commands and the five stages; no licence, no price and no statement of what leaves the machine. The plugin repository's README at commit 1a48e11 documents only a sibling plugin (evals), which fine-tunes small judge or guardrail models on the vendor's servers behind an API key.
maturity: Vendor product; no independent report read.
cost: An account; the agent's description and, optionally, production traces go to the vendor.
simpler_alternative: The kit's frozen evaluator on held-out data; for agent behaviour, deterministic task graders as in the TRL agent-traces example.
reason: A different job (testing an agent product with simulated users), a hosted service that needs an account, and judgments that are not a frozen, local evaluator. Revisit only if evaluating a deployed agent becomes part of the kit; then read the plugin's code, pin it and try it in a temporary project with the user's account.
checked: simulation.plurai.ai/connect and github.com/plurai-ai/plurai-plugins README at commit 1a48e11; 2026-11-12
